The Australian Football League (AFL)—originally known as the Victorian Football League (VFL) until it was renamed in 1990—has a rich history stretching back to the late 19th century. 

Australian rules football itself was created in Melbourne in 1858, initially as a way to keep cricketers fit during the winter months. Tom Wills, a key figure in the game's development, published the first set of rules in 1859, drawing inspiration from various football codes as well as traditional Indigenous games like *Marngrook*.

The VFL was officially established in 1896 when a group of clubs broke away from the Victorian Football Association (VFA), playing their inaugural season in 1897 with eight teams: Carlton, Collingwood, Essendon, Fitzroy, Geelong, Melbourne, St Kilda, and South Melbourne. Over the decades, the competition expanded significantly beyond Victoria, adding teams from Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales, and Queensland, which led to its national expansion and rebranding as the AFL in 1990. Today, the league features 18 clubs and remains Australia's most attended and watched sporting competition, culminating each year in the Grand Final at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG).
